transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Nair, Sam Rivera, Eliot Park, Jordan Lee, Maya Gonzalez, Tom Brooks, Lena Ortiz

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone good morning, thanks for carving time, this is the SE enablement on messaging and competitive demo practice. Um, we've got about an hour and 15 so we'll run through the new hooks, then Priya will walk the demo, we'll do two practice runs and then capture feedback.

[00:18] Priya Nair: Morning all. real quick housekeeping: recording is on, slides are in the shared drive, please drop questions in chat if you don't want to interrupt.

[00:27] Jordan Lee: sounds good, just flagging I'll need some concrete one-liners for quick discovery calls — something under 20 seconds.

[00:33] Alex Chen: Yep that's a primary ask. Sam — have the two top hooks ready?

[00:36] Sam Rivera: Yeah, I pushed two variants: one econ-first — "cut per-token inference cost with smart caching and quantization while preserving answer quality" — and one reliability-first — "predictable SLOs across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments." We can show both to shorten discovery.

[00:52] Maya Gonzalez: The econ one is nice but we need simpler language for non-technical product leads, maybe replace quantization with "model optimization"?

[00:58] Priya Nair: good point, say "model optimization" — it's less jargon heavy. Also have a version that leads with: "Ship LLM features with consistent latency and cost across environments."

[01:08] Alex Chen: Great. Ok next section: competitive positioning. We're seeing questions about debugability and model ownership, especially versus OpenAI and Anthropic. Eliot, quick overview?

[01:18] Eliot Park: Sure. Key bullets: OpenAI = strong model family, easy to adopt but limited control on custom infra, less transparent for tail latency. Anthropic emphasises safety and constitutional models; competitor messaging focuses on policy control. Cohere and AWS Bedrock offer managed infra but usually less focus on batching and cost controls. Our angle: production-first economics + unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private.

[01:40] Tom Brooks: Are we differentiating on SOC2 and KMS? Customers ask that a lot for regulated accounts.

[01:45] Alex Chen: Yes — emphasize SOC 2, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs. For private deployments mention on-prem and VPC options, and SSO/SAML + RBAC. Put that on the battlecard front and center.

[01:55] [short laughter]

[02:00] Sam Rivera: I'm adding a one-liner: "Choose how you want to run inference — hosted for fastest time-to-value, dedicated for predictable throughput, private for regulated workloads. Same API, same tooling."

[02:14] Jordan Lee: When customers push back on price vs OpenAI, we should show a demo where per-token cost drops after we enable caching and batching?

[02:21] Priya Nair: Absolutely. Demo plan: show two scenarios — 1) unsecured hosted baseline (no KV cache, default batching), and 2) optimized with prefix caching, continuous batching, and quantization profile. Walk through logs in the console to show token cost drop and latency profile.

[02:40] Maya Gonzalez: How much of the infra details do we share live? I want to avoid deep kernel/compilation talk in a standard demo.

[02:46] Priya Nair: For AE-level demos keep it high-level: "smart batching, prefix cache, and quantization" — then seed a technical follow-up with an SE deep-dive if they ask for kernel/compilation.

[02:58] Alex Chen: Ok, Priya can you run the first practice demo? We'll time it to 8 minutes. Priya, camera on? [chuckle]

[03:05] [03:05] Priya Nair: launching demo, sharing screen. I'll start with customer scenario: e-comm search assistant that reduces search latency and returns personalized suggestions.

[03:18] [03:18] Priya Nair: "We integrate Redwood to serve your product search model; the runtime uses smart caching and workload-aware batching to keep p99 latency low while reducing tokens for identical prefixes."

[03:35] Tom Brooks: can you show the console where batching metrics live?

[03:38] Priya Nair: sure, switching to Redwood Console -> Routes -> Model -> Traces. Here's the token-level cost chart, here's the latency histogram. You'll notice the orange is baseline and blue is after enabling caching. See batch size increased from avg 3 to avg 12 which reduces per-token overhead.

[03:58] [04:00] Jordan Lee: Nice, the charts are clear. Quick note — sometimes the chart labels get munged in transcription, we should label axes explicitly.

[04:08] Priya Nair: noted. Now I'll flip to a canary/rollout example: we split traffic 10/90 to a quantized variant. You can see per-token cost reduce by ~28% with a small p99 increase but within SLO.

[04:27] Maya Gonzalez: What's the customer-ready way to explain that tradeoff?

[04:30] Alex Chen: Script: "We route to a cheaper quantized model for non-critical traffic and keep the full-precision model for high-priority routes — that gets you most of the cost savings with minimal quality impact."

[04:42] [04:42] Priya Nair: ok switching to objection handling — data residency. If they require on-prem, we talk about Private deployment, VPC or on-prem package, and KMS integration for key control. If they want audit trail, show audit logs in Console.

[05:00] [05:00] Jordan Lee: good — also confirm SOC2 and ISO roadmap?

[05:04] Alex Chen: SOC 2 Type II done, ISO 27001 in progress (Q3), add that to the battlecard.

[05:12] Eliot Park: I'll update the compliance slide.

[05:16] Priya Nair: quick feedback loop: for the demo pacing, callouts should be 6 to 8 seconds, don't linger on charts more than 25 seconds unless asked.

[05:26] Alex Chen: Ok let's do feedback for this run. Jordan?

[05:29] Jordan Lee: Strong. Suggestion: open with a one-liner that ties to buyer metric — "reduce search latency by X and inference cost by Y" — numbers or percent ranges help.

[05:38] Maya Gonzalez: Also have a fallback phrase when they say "we use OpenAI" — e.g., "OpenAI is great for prototyping; if you need predictable unit economics and enterprise controls, Redwood gives you that same API plus dedicated/private options and SLAs."

[05:55] [crosstalk]

[06:00] Alex Chen: Good. Priya will do another run focusing on the 20-second opening, then we'll role-play a pricing objection.

[06:08] [06:08] Priya Nair: Ok second run: 20-second opener — "Many teams start on hosted models but hit unpredictable costs at scale. Redwood gives you consistent latency and the levers — batching, caching, quantization, and routing — to control unit economics without rewiring your stack."

[06:31] Tom Brooks: I like the levers line. Maybe simplify to 'levers to control cost and latency' so it's short.

[06:36] Priya Nair: noted. Now role-play: Jordan, you're the buyer pushing back on price.

[06:40] [06:40] Jordan Lee: Sure. "We tried other APIs, they're cheaper per-token, why should we pay more?"

[06:44] Priya Nair: "Great question. Ticket: Many providers show a low per-token price but that doesn't account for real-world costs — tail latency, re-requests, and the lack of smart batching and cache. With Redwood you get optimizations built-in that reduce the total inference bill and predictable SLOs for customer-facing features."

[07:03] Maya Gonzalez: Nice — add a concrete example: on a 1M qps workload we typically see 20-30% savings after caching/batching. Don't lock to exact numbers unless validated.

[07:15] Priya Nair: I'll say 'typical ranges' unless we have a benchmark sheet.

[07:19] Alex Chen: Action item for Sam: add a small benchmark section with ranges and a note 'varies by workload; run a quick pilot for exacts'.

[07:28] Sam Rivera: will do.

[07:32] [07:32] Eliot Park: quick note about competitor scripts: when they say "OpenAI has better models" we pivot to the use case — "If you need bleeding-edge capabilities, we often recommend open model stacks, but for shipped customer features where latency/cost and compliance matter, Redwood adds the runtime and controls."

[07:50] Jordan Lee: switch to a tricky Q: 'What about hallucinations?'

[07:54] Priya Nair: For hallucinations: talk about evals, prompt engineering, reranking, and the ability to pin model versions and run continuous evals. Show the evals dashboard briefly.

[08:06] Maya Gonzalez: Keep that high-level unless it's a research customer.

[08:10] Alex Chen: Ok we're about 8 minutes in demo territory; moving on to role-play the canary rollback. Priya, simulate a canary failing quality check.

[08:20] [08:20] Priya Nair: Starting canary example: canary gets 10% traffic, quality metric drops 2.5% vs baseline — automatic rollback triggers and an alert to the team, traffic shifts back immediately.

[08:38] Tom Brooks: Customers will ask how we measure quality — define 'quality metric' in the script: perplexity? NPS of results? Clickthrough?

[08:44] Priya Nair: say 'application-specific metrics like clickthrough or success rate, plus automated regression checks on prompt sets.'

[08:52] Alex Chen: Good. Quick pulse — any major gaps?

[08:56] Maya Gonzalez: We should prep a short legal/SC reply for enterprise procurement around data retention.

[09:02] Alex Chen: Action item: Priya and Tom to draft a procurement FAQ.

[09:08] [09:08] Priya Nair: One last practice run working through the handshake script: discovery question set, three opening hooks, demo cadence, pricing ask, and next steps.

[09:20] [09:20] Priya Nair: Start discovery: "What's your current inference stack? throughput and latency SLOs? any compliance constraints? what's success after 90 days?"

[09:32] Jordan Lee: good, add 'who's the decision maker' and 'budget owner' to the discovery.

[09:36] Priya Nair: Noted. Handshake script close: "If this resonates, we can run a two-week pilot to collect actual metrics and savings estimates, then scope Dedicated if needed."

[09:49] Alex Chen: wrap up time. Quick recap of next steps and owners. I'll send the updated messaging doc and the recorded practice to the enablement Slack channel. Eliot will update the battlecard. Sam will add benchmark ranges. Priya will post the demo script and record the practice video. Tom will update CRM.

[10:10] Maya Gonzalez: Can we get a short 1-pager 'fight card' for quick reference?

[10:14] Sam Rivera: yes, I'll produce a 1-page battlecard with objection scripts and data points.

[10:20] Alex Chen: Thanks folks. Any last minute?

[10:22] Lena Ortiz: just one — can we add a "quick ask" cheat sheet for SDRs? two lines: open, qualify, close.

[10:28] Alex Chen: Yep — add to action items. Ok meeting over, thanks.
